ProximalLangevin/Corrections.lean.title: Exact algebraic corrections and an averaged-proximity counterexample
ProximalLangevin/Corrections.lean.summary: This module contains explicit mathematical certificates. Each claim is limited to its stated algebraic example or implication; these certificates do not claim that every stronger result in the reference paper is false.

steps.title: The quadratic proximal expansion has positive second order
steps.body:
On page 15, v3 equation (22) prints a negative second-order term in the proximal expansion. Differentiating \(p+\lambda\nabla g_2(p)=x\) gives a positive second derivative contribution. The scalar quadratic supplies an exact certificate:

\[ \operatorname{prox}_{u^2/2}^\lambda(x) =\frac{x}{1+\lambda} =x-\lambda x+\lambda^2x-\frac{\lambda^3x}{1+\lambda}. \]

The negative second-order expression leaves an error at least \(\lambda^2\) when \(x=1\), so it cannot be that quadratic's third-order expansion. This diagnoses the displayed algebra; the quadratic is not globally Lipschitz and is not by itself a counterexample to the full final theorem under A3.

Separately, twice differentiability almost everywhere and the stated moment bound do not supply a uniform integrable third-order remainder. The original \(O(\lambda)\) minimizer claim is therefore not reproduced here. The proved uniform-gap argument replaces it with \(\sqrt{\lambda K^2/m}\). A proof gap does not establish that the stronger conclusion is false.

steps.title: Squared scaling and the geometric endpoint
steps.body: Norm homogeneity gives \(\|Ng\|^2=N^2\|g\|^2\). The numerical case \(N=2,\|g\|=1\) disproves linear squared-gradient scaling. Substituting \(\lambda=\gamma/(1-\mu\gamma)\) gives \(1-q=0\). Lean’s total real division has \(1/0=0\); the numerical certificate \(1\not\le0+1/(1-1)\) shows why an unguarded formula at that endpoint cannot express an error floor.

steps.title: The proximal deficit carries an inverse step factor
steps.body: If \(\langle x-y,p(x)-p(y)\rangle\le(1-\mu)\|x-y\|^2\), expand the residual difference \(R(x)-R(y)=\gamma^{-1}[(x-y)-(p(x)-p(y))]\). For \(\gamma>0\), this proves \(\langle x-y,R(x)-R(y)\rangle\ge(\mu/\gamma)\|x-y\|^2\). The modulus is \(\mu/\gamma\), rather than \(\mu\).

steps.title: A shared parameter prevents the lifted-proximal identity
steps.body:
Use the convex pair function \(g(\theta,x)=|\theta-x|\) and unit proximal parameter. The actual pair objectives show that inputs \((1,0)\) and \((1,4)\) have minimizers \((1/2,1/2)\) and \((2,3)\). Averaging their parameter outputs gives \((5/4,1/2,3)\). The shared lifted objective is

\[\tfrac12(|\theta-x_1|+|\theta-x_2|)+\tfrac12(\theta-1)^2+\tfrac14(x_1^2+(x_2-4)^2).\]

Direct absolute-value inequalities certify the two pair minima. Exact arithmetic shows that the competitor \((1,1,3)\) has strictly smaller shared objective than the averaged output. Therefore averaged pairwise proximity is not in general the proximal map of the lifted sum.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldDrift.lean.title: The actual mean-field force is Lipschitz in W₂
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldDrift.lean.summary: For a pair potential \(V\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, define \(b_V(\theta,\mu)=\int\nabla_\theta V(\theta,x)\mu(dx)\). The measures are probability laws with finite second moments. Every Bochner expectation and every finite real transport distance is justified.

steps.title: A Lipschitz observable preserves L² and controls expectation differences
steps.body:
Center an observable \(\phi\) at \(\phi(0)\); its norm growth is bounded by \(K\|x\|\), so \(\phi(X)\in L^2\subset L^1\). Given any finite-cost coupling \(c\) of \(\mu, u\), pushforward integration and Cauchy–Schwarz give

\[\left\|\int\phi\,d\mu-\int\phi\,d u ight\|\le K\left(\int\|x-y\|^2dc ight)^{1/2}.\]

Taking the actual coupling infimum yields the bound \(K W_2(\mu, u)\), with finiteness supplied by the second moments.

steps.title: Project the true joint gradient to its parameter block
steps.body: The bounded linear map \(P_\theta\) keeps the parameter coordinates. Its squared norm is a sub-sum of the full Euclidean square, hence \(\|P_\theta z\|\le\|z\|\). Define \(\phi_\theta(x)=P_\theta\nabla V(\theta,x)\), then define the mean-field force as its actual Bochner integral. These definitions use the existing joint potential, with no arbitrary force field substituted for its gradient.

steps.title: Control joint parameter and latent perturbations
steps.body:
Decompose a joint pair difference into its two coordinate inclusions, giving \(\|(\theta,x)-(\theta',x')\|\le\|\theta-\theta'\|+\|x-x'\|\). Gradient Lipschitzness and the nonexpansive parameter projection imply

\[\|\phi_\theta(x)-\phi_{\theta'}(x')\|\le L(\|\theta-\theta'\|+\|x-x'\|).\]

Fixing \(\theta=\theta'\) proves that the latent observable itself is \(L\)-Lipschitz.

steps.title: Separate the parameter change from the law change
steps.body:
For a differentiable potential \(V\), define

\[ b_V(\theta,\mu)=\int \nabla_\theta V(\theta,x)\,\mu(dx). \]

Assume \(\nabla V\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu,\nu\) are probability laws with finite second moment. Coordinate projection has norm at most one, so the integrand is Lipschitz and grows at most linearly. Its Bochner expectation is therefore integrable. For any finite-cost coupling, compare its two integrands, apply the norm-of-integral inequality, and use Cauchy–Schwarz. Taking the infimum of actual coupling costs gives

\[ \|b_V(\theta,\mu)-b_V(\theta',\nu)\| \le L\bigl(\|\theta-\theta'\|+W_2(\mu,\nu)\bigr). \]

With the genuine split envelope \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), the proved constant is \(L_1+1/\eta\). The paper’s \(1/\eta\) constant applies to a full envelope, not to this split expression in general. This is a corrected W₂ version of Lemma C.1: its right-hand side is weaker than the paper’s W₁ statement, and the distinction is explicit. Propositions C.2–C.3 are not consequences formalized by this lemma alone.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldProcess.lean.title: Construct the mean-field L² integral equations
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldProcess.lean.summary: Work on a probability space \(Q\), with \(H=L^2(Q;\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x})\). A potential \(V\) with globally \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient defines the actual mean-field drift. Its continuous finite-horizon integral solution is constructed by the Banach-space Picard theorem.

steps.title: Expectation is a bounded linear map from L²
steps.body: The norm-of-integral inequality and \(\|X\|_{L^1}\le\|X\|_{L^2}\) on a probability space give \(\|\mathbb E_Q X\|\le\|X\|_2\). Bochner additivity and scalar linearity therefore define a bounded linear map \(\mathcal E:H\to E\) with operator norm at most one. The evaluation lemma records that its value is the actual integral.

steps.title: Coordinate projections and a parameter inclusion
steps.body: Define \(P_x(\theta,x)=x\) and \(I_\theta(\theta)=(\theta,0)\). Their coordinate identities follow by evaluating the definitions. The Euclidean square identity \(\|(\theta,0)\|^2=\|\theta\|^2\), followed by nonnegative square-root cancellation, proves that \(I_\theta\) is an isometry.

steps.title: A true latent mask erases all parameter coordinates
steps.body: Set \(M_x=I-I_\theta P_\theta\). Its parameter block is zero and its latent block is unchanged. Expanding the Euclidean squared norm shows \(\|M_xz\|^2\le\|z\|^2\), since the discarded parameter square is nonnegative. Thus the mask is nonexpansive and remains bounded after composition on \(L^2\).

steps.title: Average exactly the parameter block
steps.body:
Construct the bounded linear map

\[\mathcal M X=\operatorname{const}(I_\theta P_\theta\mathbb E_QX)+M_xX.\]

The expectation estimate and coordinate contractions bound each term by \(\|X\|_2\), so \(\|\mathcal M X\|_2\le2\|X\|_2\). Linearity then proves \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal M)\le2\). This is a conservative sufficient constant.

steps.title: Define the actual drift and apply Picard
steps.body:
Set \(\mathcal A_V(X)=\mathcal M(\nabla V(X))\). The Nemytskii map for the actual Lipschitz gradient preserves \(L^2\) and has constant \(L\), so \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_V)\le2L\). For any continuous \(H\)-valued input \(B\) with \(B_0=0\), and any \(T\ge0\), Picard constructs continuous \(Y\) with \(Y_0=Y^{\rm in}\) and

\[Y_t-Y^{\rm in}=-\int_0^t\mathcal A_V(Y_s)ds+B_t,\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

The proof is an existence theorem in the actual complete Banach space \(H\).

steps.title: Verify the intended block formulas in L²
steps.body:
Almost everywhere representative equalities show

\[(\mathcal M X)(\omega)=(\mathbb E_Q P_\theta X,\,P_xX(\omega)).\]

Applying parameter projection gives the constant random variable \(\operatorname{const}(P_\theta\mathbb E_QX)\); applying latent projection gives \(P_xX\). The proofs explicitly combine the almost everywhere addition, constant and composition identities, so they are equalities in \(L^2\).

steps.title: Identify the parameter force with the true marginal integral
steps.body:
Define \(a_V(X)=P_ heta\mathbb E_Q abla V(X)\), a continuous map on \(H\). The drift blocks are \(\operatorname{const}(a_V(X))\) and \(P_x abla V(X)\). If \(P_ heta X=\operatorname{const}( heta)\), reconstruct \(X=( heta,P_xX)\) almost everywhere. Commute the bounded projection through expectation and use the pushforward integral formula to prove

\[a_V(X)=\int abla_ heta V( heta,x)\,\mathcal L_Q(P_xX)(dx).\]

steps.title: Project the integral equation and construct a deterministic parameter
steps.body:
Suppose the initial parameter is constant \(\theta_0\) and \(P_\theta B_t=0\). Bounded linear maps commute with the Bochner time integral, so projecting the constructed equation gives \(P_\theta Y_t=\operatorname{const}(\theta_t)\), where \(\theta_t=\theta_0-\int_0^t a_V(Y_s)ds\). The continuous primitive proves continuity of \(\theta\). Set \(\mu_t=\mathcal L_Q(P_xY_t)\) and insert the force identity:

\[\theta_t-\theta_0=-\int_0^t b_V(\theta_s,\mu_s)ds,\qquad P_xY_t-P_xY_0=-\int_0^tP_x\nabla V(Y_s)ds+P_xB_t.\]

Both identities hold in their stated deterministic or \(L^2\) sense on the finite horizon.

steps.title: Construct a continuous latent-only Brownian input
steps.body: Apply the latent mask to the actual coordinate Brownian \(L^2\) noise. Brownian second moments prove its continuity in \(L^2\) and its zero value at time zero. Masking makes its parameter projection zero at every time. No separate continuity assumption on a stochastic error process is used.

steps.title: Specialize to Brownian input and to the split envelope
steps.body: The constructed Brownian input satisfies all hypotheses of the general integral existence theorem, so substitution gives the Brownian-driven \(L^2\) solution. For \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), the actual proximal calculus supplies the Lipschitz gradient constant \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\), which is included as a derived witness in the conclusion. These results establish continuous \(L^2\) integral equations; they do not assert a pathwise strong-SDE or a Fokker–Planck PDE theorem.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldSmoothing.lean.title: Finite smoothing comparison for actual mean-field equations
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldSmoothing.lean.summary: For this module the convex bounded-below \(g_2\) is additionally differentiable, with \(L_2\)-Lipschitz gradient and global value Lipschitz constant \(K\). The finite-horizon comparison uses the same initialization and additive input for the original and split-smoothed systems.

steps.title: At differentiability points subgradients equal the gradient
steps.body: A supporting vector \(s\) makes \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle s,x angle\) globally minimized at the support point \(p\). Its derivative there is zero, so \(s= abla f(p)\). Apply this to the genuine proximal residual to obtain the exact identity \( abla f^\eta(x)= abla f(P_\eta(x))\).

steps.title: Smoothness gives a finite score defect
steps.body:
Compose \( abla f\), which is \(L_2\)-Lipschitz, with the nonexpansive map \(P_\eta\). The envelope gradient therefore has constant \(L_2\), independent of \(\eta\). The actual proximal displacement bound \(\|x-P_\eta(x)\|\le\eta K\) gives

\[\| abla f(x)- abla f^\eta(x)\|\le L_2\|x-P_\eta(x)\|\le\eta L_2K.\]

This is a finite inequality, without a Taylor remainder.

steps.title: Recover component regularity from the regular sum
steps.body: If \(U=f+g\) and \(f\) are differentiable, then \(g=U-f\) is differentiable. Gradient linearity gives \( abla g= abla U- abla f\), so gradient constants add: \(\operatorname{Lip}( abla g)\le L_U+L_f\). This provides a legitimate \(L_2\) when only the original sum and the smooth part were specified.

steps.title: Cancel the common additive input before Grönwall
steps.body:
For integral solutions with drifts \(g,k\), the same input \(B\), initial states \(x,y\), and \(\sup_z\|g(z)-k(z)\|\le\varepsilon\), subtract their equations. The input cancels exactly and the drift difference is at most \(L\|Y-Z\|+\varepsilon\). Integral Grönwall gives

\[\|Y_t-Z_t\|\le e^{Lt}\|x-y\|+\varepsilon\Psi(L,t),\qquad\Psi(L,t)=\begin{cases}(e^{Lt}-1)/L,&L\ne0,\\t,&L=0.\end{cases}\]

This estimate requires no differentiation of \(B\).

steps.title: Construct both actual systems and quantify the smoothing error
steps.body:
For this result, additionally assume \(g_2\) is differentiable with an \(L_2\)-Lipschitz gradient, while retaining convexity, the lower bound and the global value Lipschitz constant \(K\). The supporting subgradient at a differentiability point must equal the actual gradient. Proximal optimality therefore gives the exact identity

\[ \nabla g_2^\eta(v)=\nabla g_2(P_\eta(v)). \]

Nonexpansiveness of \(P_\eta\) preserves the smooth-score constant \(L_2\), and \(\|v-P_\eta(v)\|\le\eta K\) gives the finite score defect

\[ \|\nabla g_2(v)-\nabla g_2^\eta(v)\|\le\eta L_2K. \]

No asymptotic expansion or integrated remainder is used. If the original sum \(U=g_1+g_2\) is differentiable with \(L_U\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g_1\) has constant \(L_1\), the component regularity is derived with \(L_2=L_U+L_1\).

The development constructs original and split-smoothed L² integral solutions with the same initialization and additive input. Their input cancels. The actual drift operators differ by at most \(2\eta L_2K\), and their common gradient constant is at most \(L_1+L_2\), independently of \(\eta\). Grönwall gives

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\|Y_t-Z_t\|_{L^2} \le 2\eta L_2K\,\Psi(2(L_1+L_2),T), \qquad \Psi(a,T)=\begin{cases}(e^{aT}-1)/a,&a>0,\\T,&a=0.\end{cases} \]

Specialize the shared initialization to a constant parameter and the shared input to the latent-only Brownian construction to obtain the usual deterministic-parameter mean-field systems. The proved norm is the supremum over time of L² norms. It is not the expectation of a pathwise supremum in Proposition C.3. This is a consistent split-smoothing replacement with explicit assumptions and a finite linear-in-\(\eta\) norm bound.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldVariance.lean.title: Exact iid variance and the empirical parameter force
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldVariance.lean.summary: On a probability space, square-integrable Hilbert-valued variables have integrable inner products. On the actual finite product law, independent centered samples yield an exact \(1/N\) variance identity.

steps.title: Cancel every off-diagonal covariance
steps.body:
Realize the supplied \(L^2\) functions as \(L^2\) elements; Cauchy–Schwarz gives integrable pairwise inner products. Expand

\[\mathbb E\left\|\sum_iX_i\right\|^2=\sum_{i,j}\mathbb E\langle X_i,X_j\rangle.\]

For \(i\ne j\), independence factors the expectation into \(\langle\mathbb E X_i,\mathbb E X_j\rangle=0\). The diagonal terms are \(\mathbb E\|X_i\|^2\). Finite sums and established integrability justify the expansion.

steps.title: Use the actual finite product for an exact sample-mean variance
steps.body:
For a square-integrable observable \(\phi\) and a probability law \(\mu\), the finite product measure \(\mu^{\otimes N}\) constructs the independent samples. The proof centers \(\phi\), expands the squared Hilbert norm, and uses independence and zero mean to cancel every off-diagonal inner product. The exact result is

\[ \mathbb E_{\mu^{\otimes N}} \left\|\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi(X_i)-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\right\|^2 =\frac1N\mathbb E_\mu\|\phi-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\|^2. \]

Taking square roots proves the \(N^{-1/2}\) sampling factor. The actual parameter-gradient observable is square integrable under finite-P₂ latent laws, so the formula applies to the mean-field force.

The source’s exchangeability premise alone does not cancel these covariances. A quantitative chaos estimate needs controlled initialization, such as the actual iid construction used here. This exact sampling identity is a proved ingredient; by itself it is not a propagation-of-chaos theorem.

steps.title: Specialize the variance to a true gradient observable
steps.body:
Fix \( heta\) and let \(\phi(x)= abla_ heta U( heta,x)\). A Lipschitz joint gradient makes this observable Lipschitz, hence square integrable under any finite-second-moment latent law \(\mu\). Its expectation is exactly \(b_U( heta,\mu)\). Substitute into the iid formula to obtain

\[\mathbb E\left\| rac1N\sum_i abla_ heta U( heta,X_i)-b_U( heta,\mu) ight\|^2= rac1N\mathbb E\| abla_ heta U( heta,X)-b_U( heta,\mu)\|^2.\]

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticleDrift..title: Construct the physical particle drift in a coordinate L² space
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticleDrift..summary: Let \(H_N=L^2(P;\Theta)\times\prod_{i

steps.title: Coordinate inclusions and nonexpansive projections
steps.body: Define the coordinate product state and the latent inclusion \(I_x(x)=(0,x)\). The Euclidean square proves \(\|I_xx\|=\|x\|\), while the latent projection has norm at most one. For any bounded linear pointwise contraction \(C\), integrating \(\|C(X)\|^2\le\|X\|^2\) proves \(\|C\circ X\|_2\le\|X\|_2\).

steps.title: Assemble one actual joint random pair
steps.body:
Set \(J(\Theta,X)=I_\theta\Theta+I_xX\). Its representative is the genuine pair \((\Theta(\omega),X(\omega))\) almost everywhere. Linearity of the inclusions and their norm bounds give

\[\|J(\Theta,X)-J(\Theta',X')\|_2\le\|\Theta-\Theta'\|_2+\|X-X'\|_2.\]

steps.title: Define the gradient and empirical particle drift
steps.body:
Apply the actual gradient \( abla V\) to each pair \(J(\Theta,X_i)\). The parameter force is the empirical average and each latent force is its own gradient block:

\[\mathcal A_N(z)=\left( rac1N\sum_i abla_ heta V(\Theta,X_i),\ ( abla_xV(\Theta,X_i))_i ight).\]

Almost everywhere composition and finite-sum identities verify these exact coordinate formulas. The definition does not replace the empirical parameter force by a mean-field expectation.

steps.title: Dimension-free Lipschitz control constructs the actual solution
steps.body: Each coordinate difference is bounded by the product-state norm. The joint-pair estimate therefore gives \(\|\nabla V(J_i z)-\nabla V(J_i w)\|_2\le2L\|z-w\|\). Averaging \(N\) parameter terms and dividing by \(N>0\) preserves this bound; the maximum of the latent terms also preserves it. Hence \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_N)\le2L\), independently of \(N\). Picard constructs continuous \(Z\) satisfying \(Z_t-Z_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal A_N(Z_s)ds+B_t\) for any continuous input with \(B_0=0\).

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCopies.lean.title: Actual iid L² copies and their exact drift residual
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCopies.lean.summary: Starting from one mean-field random pair on \(Q\), construct copies on the actual finite product \(P=Q^{\otimes N}\). When its parameter is deterministic, all copies share that parameter and their latent coordinates are iid.

steps.title: Measure-preserving coordinate pullback is a bounded linear copy map
steps.body: For product coordinate \(\omega_i\), define \(C_iX=X\circ\omega_i\). Evaluation is measure preserving, so pullback is an \(L^2\) isometry and a bounded linear map. Its representative equals \(X(\omega_i)\) almost everywhere. Coordinate substitution proves \(C_i(CX)=C(C_iX)\) for bounded linear \(C\), and \(C_i(\operatorname{const}x)=\operatorname{const}x\).

steps.title: Center and compute the true empirical fluctuation norm
steps.body:
For \(N>0\), define \(\mathcal C X=X-\operatorname{const}(\mathbb EX)\) and \(\Delta_N(X)=N^{-1}\sum_iC_iX-\operatorname{const}(\mathbb EX)\). Almost everywhere finite-sum identities identify its representative with the genuine sample mean. The exact iid variance formula gives

\[\|\Delta_N(X)\|_{L^2(P)}^2=\frac1N\|\mathcal C X\|_{L^2(Q)}^2,\qquad\|\Delta_N(X)\|_2=\frac{\|\mathcal C X\|_2}{\sqrt N}.\]

steps.title: Build the reference particle state without altering its parameter
steps.body:
Bounded linear maps commute with actual Bochner expectation, and constants have their stated expectation on a probability space. Define

\[\mathcal R_N(X)=\left(\operatorname{const}(\mathbb E P_\theta X),\ (P_xC_iX)_i\right).\]

If \(P_\theta X=\operatorname{const}\theta\), the parameter block of \(\mathcal R_N(X)\) is exactly \(\operatorname{const}\theta\). The coordinate lemmas are direct evaluations of this bounded linear construction.

steps.title: Reconstruct each reference pair and commute the true drift
steps.body: Reassembling a variable from its parameter and latent projections returns the same \(L^2\) element. With deterministic parameter this proves \(J_i\mathcal R_N(X)=C_iX\). A Lipschitz pointwise drift also commutes with coordinate pullback, since both representatives are the same function \(b(X(\omega_i))\) almost everywhere.

steps.title: Only the empirical parameter block remains in the residual
steps.body:
Apply the particle drift to \(\mathcal R_N(X)\), and compare with \(\mathcal R_N(\mathcal A_V(X))\). Each latent block agrees exactly by the preceding commutation. The parameter difference is the centered empirical gradient:

\[\mathcal A_N(\mathcal R_NX)-\mathcal R_N(\mathcal A_VX)=\left(\Delta_N(P_\theta\nabla V(X)),0\right).\]

The product maximum norm and exact fluctuation identity therefore give residual norm \(\|\mathcal C(P_\theta\nabla V(X))\|_2/\sqrt N\). This equality is the source of the particle comparison rate.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldForcing.lean.title: Grönwall comparison with an extra continuous noise input
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldForcing.lean.summary: In a Banach space let \(F\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. Compare actual integral equations with a common input \(B\), one extra continuous input \(A\), and a reference forcing \(G\) satisfying a finite drift defect.

steps.title: Subtract the extra input before applying integral Grönwall
steps.body:
Suppose \(\|A_t\|\le a\), \(\|F(Y_t)-G_t\|\le C\), and

\[X_t-x=-\int_0^tF(X_s)ds+B_t+A_t,\qquad Y_t-x=-\int_0^tG_sds+B_t.\]

Set \(D_t=X_t-Y_t-A_t\). The common input cancels and \(\|D_t\|\le\int_0^t[L\|D_s\|+La+C]ds\). Grönwall yields \(\|X_t-Y_t\|\le(C+La)\Psi(L,T)+a\) on \([0,T]\). The proof uses continuous integral equations and never differentiates the additional input.

steps.title: Factor a common inverse sampling scale
steps.body:
The explicit zero-initial-error Grönwall function is linear in its forcing coefficient, including its \(L=0\) branch. Thus \(\operatorname{GB}(0,L,C/r,T)=\operatorname{GB}(0,L,C,T)/r\). If \(r>0\), \(\|A_t\|\le a/r\) and \(\|F(Y_t)-G_t\|\le C/r\), substitute into the preceding theorem and factor:

\[\|X_t-Y_t\|\le\frac{(C+La)\Psi(L,T)+a}{r}.\]

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldNoise.lean.title: Construct the empirical parameter Brownian input
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldNoise.lean.summary: On \(Q^{\otimes N}\), \(N>0\), use copy zero of a supplied \(d_\theta\)-coordinate Brownian source for the common parameter input. The actual noise amplitude is \(\sqrt{2/N}\).

steps.title: Pull back Brownian coordinates and define their scaled L² noise
steps.body: Coordinate evaluation on the finite product is measure preserving, so each pulled-back scalar process retains its standard Brownian law. Define \(A_t=N^{-1/2}\sqrt2(B_t^\theta-B_0^\theta)\) as an actual \(L^2\) element. The Brownian-noise construction proves continuity in \(L^2\) and value zero at time zero; scalar multiplication preserves both facts.

steps.title: Derive the exact norm and its N-independent horizon coefficient
steps.body:
The coordinate second moments sum to \(d_\theta t\). Consequently

\[\|A_t\|_2=\frac{\sqrt{2d_\theta}\sqrt t}{\sqrt N}\le\frac{\sqrt{2d_\theta}\sqrt T}{\sqrt N},\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

The theorem follows by the exact Brownian norm identity and monotonicity of the square root. The canonical specialization uses the already constructed Gaussian time-indicator Brownian source, so it supplies a concrete instance rather than postulating one.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldBrownianFamily.title: An independent Brownian family for all actual particle coordinates
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldBrownianFamily.summary: On \(Q^{\otimes N}\), choose parameter Brownian coordinates from copy zero and latent coordinate \((i,j)\) from copy \(i\). Injective selection proves independence of complete selected coordinate paths.

steps.title: Select distinct copy/coordinate pairs
steps.body: Map a parameter index \(j\) to \((0,\mathrm{parameter}\ j)\), and a latent index \((i,j)\) to \((i,\mathrm{latent}\ j)\). The parameter/latent tags make the two kinds disjoint, and equality within either kind forces equality of the original indices. This proves injectivity. Define the family by evaluating the corresponding source Brownian coordinate in the selected copy; the displayed coordinate identities unfold the selection.

steps.title: Each selected process retains its Brownian law
steps.body: Pullback along product evaluation is measure preserving, so every selected scalar process is standard pre-Brownian. If all source evaluations are measurable, composition with the selected coordinate map proves every new evaluation measurable as well.

steps.title: Flatten independent rows and select an injective subfamily
steps.body: The finite product makes the complete Brownian rows independent. Inside each row, the supplied full coordinate paths are independent. The product-family independence theorem flattens these into independent variables indexed by \((i,j)\). Precomposing with the injective selection proves independence of all particle coordinates, including parameter and first-particle latent blocks. The canonical Brownian source supplies both the row laws and full-path independence, yielding an explicit complete family.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldInitialSource..title: Concrete independent initialization and Brownian paths
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldInitialSource..summary: Given a latent probability law \(\mu\) with finite second moment and a deterministic \(\theta_0\), use the product \(Q=\mu\otimes Q_B\), where \(Q_B\) is the canonical joint Brownian source. This constructs all initialization and source hypotheses from primitive data.

steps.title: Product source and its measurable Brownian evaluations
steps.body:
The source is the actual product law \(\mu\otimes Q_B\). Brownian coordinates use only its second factor, so measure-preserving second projection transfers their standard Brownian laws. Coordinate measurability assembles into full-path measurability. The joint path pushforward remains exactly its canonical product law, proving independence of the complete coordinate paths after initialization is added.

The named probability instance follows from the product measure identity \(Q(\Omega)=\mu(X)Q_B(\Omega_B)=1\cdot1=1\). This records normalization of the constructed source before any law or expectation is used.

steps.title: Build the square-integrable pair initialization
steps.body: The map \(x\mapsto(\theta_0,x)\) is nonexpansive because its parameter difference vanishes. The latent first-factor variable has finite second moment under the product law. Lipschitz composition therefore proves that \((\theta_0,X_0)\) is square integrable, and its actual \(L^2\) representative defines the initialization.

steps.title: Retain the exact parameter, latent law and source independence
steps.body: The representative equals \((\theta_0,\omega_1)\) almost everywhere, so its parameter projection is \(\operatorname{const}\theta_0\), and its latent pushforward is exactly \(\mu\). The whole initialization depends only on the first factor while all Brownian paths depend only on the second. Product independence, followed by the almost everywhere representative substitution, proves independence of initialization and the entire Brownian family.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticles.lean.title: Constructed iid particle comparison with uniform timewise L² control
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticles.lean.summary: For a potential with globally \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, compare a constructed mean-field solution with actual finite-particle coordinate solutions on the iid product source. The coefficient is chosen before all particle counts and the norm is the supremum of timewise \(L^2\) errors.

steps.title: The actual centered force is continuous and bounded on a finite horizon
steps.body: Define \(\mathcal C_V(X)=P_\theta\nabla V(X)-\operatorname{const}\mathbb E[P_\theta\nabla V(X)]\) using bounded linear centering and the actual Lipschitz drift. This composition is continuous. For continuous \(Y_t\), the image of compact \([0,T]\) is compact; its centered-force norm therefore has a finite bound \(C\ge0\). This \(C\) depends on the reference and horizon and is chosen independently of \(N\).

steps.title: Copies inherit the actual equation by bounded linearity
steps.body:
The copy map \(\mathcal R_N\) is bounded linear, so it commutes with the Bochner time integral and preserves differences. Apply it to the mean-field equation to get the exact copied-reference forcing. Define

\[C_T=2\big[(C+2Lb)\Psi(2L,T)+b\big].\]

Here \(C\) bounds the actual centered force and \(b/\sqrt N\) bounds the extra parameter input. The factor two converts the coordinate maximum norm into the sum of parameter and one latent error.

steps.title: Construct the particle solution and use the exact iid residual
steps.body:
For each \(N>0\), Picard constructs the actual particle solution \(Z\) with copied latent input and any continuous extra parameter input \(A\) bounded by \(b/\sqrt N\). The copied mean-field reference has drift residual norm exactly \(\|\mathcal C_V(Y_t)\|_2/\sqrt N\le C/\sqrt N\). Apply the forcing-comparison theorem to the \(2L\)-Lipschitz particle drift. Both tagged coordinate errors are at most the product-state norm, hence

\[\|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\le C_T/\sqrt N,\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

The theorem retains the constructed integral equation and exact iid initial state. It does not assume the final rate.

steps.title: Construct both systems with actual Brownian inputs
steps.body:
The actual centered reference force is a continuous L²-valued function of time. Compactness of \([0,T]\) supplies a finite \(C\ge0\) such that

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\| \nabla_\theta V(Y_t)-\mathbb E_Q\nabla_\theta V(Y_t)\|_2\le C. \]

This \(C\) is chosen before the quantifier over all particle counts; it depends on the reference potential, initial law and horizon, not on \(N\). Subtract the common latent input and the extra parameter Brownian input in the actual integral equations. The proof applies Grönwall to the remaining drift integral, so it never differentiates Brownian noise. Define

\[ \Psi(a,T)=\begin{cases}(e^{aT}-1)/a,&a>0,\\T,&a=0,\end{cases} \qquad C_T=2\big[(C+2Lb)\Psi(2L,T)+b\big]. \]

For every \(N>0\), the theorem constructs the actual particle integral solution with the prescribed iid initialization and proves, for every tagged particle \(i\),

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\left( \|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\right) \le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N}. \]

For the actual split-smoothed potential \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), use the derived constant \(L=L_1+1/\eta\). The coefficient can depend on \(\eta\); uniformity in smoothing is not claimed. This is a constructed iid propagation-of-chaos replacement in uniform timewise L² norm. It does not move the time supremum inside the expectation, as in printed Proposition C.2; the expected path-supremum norm is stronger; the proved uniform timewise L² estimate does not establish it.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCanonical.lean.title: Canonical finite-particle comparison from primitive latent data
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCanonical.lean.summary: Given a finite-second-moment latent law \(\mu\), deterministic \(\theta_0\), globally Lipschitz \(\nabla V\), and \(T\ge0\), the initialized canonical product source supplies concrete independent Brownian inputs and actual integral solutions for all \(N>0\).

steps.title: Discharge every scalar Brownian law and full-path independence
steps.body: The initialized source already has the true Brownian coordinate laws and independent full paths. The injective particle-coordinate selection on its finite product preserves both properties. Thus the parameter coordinates and every particle’s latent coordinates form one independent standard Brownian family, including the first-copy overlap resolved by distinct coordinate tags.

steps.title: Construct the reference once, then every particle process
steps.body:
Use the actual initial pair \((\theta_0,X_0)\) on \(\mu\otimes Q_B\), whose square integrability and deterministic parameter projection were proved. Substitute this source and the actual Brownian coordinate process into the Brownian comparison theorem. It constructs continuous \(Y,\theta\), a finite \(C\ge0\), and for every \(N>0\) a continuous actual particle solution \(Z^N\) with exact iid initialization. The equations retain latent noise \(\sqrt2 B^{x,i}\) and parameter noise \(\sqrt{2/N}B^\theta\), and prove

\[\sup_{0\le t\le T}\big(\|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\big)\le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N}.\]

The coefficient is selected before the quantifier over \(N\). This controls the supremum of \(L^2\) norms, without claiming an expected path supremum.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticleLaw.le.title: One-time Wasserstein convergence for actual tagged particles
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticleLaw.le.summary: The constructed particle/reference pair supplies an actual finite-cost coupling of tagged one-time laws. This module transfers the proved timewise \(L^2\) rate to \(W_2\), keeping the original integral equations and initialization.

steps.title: A measure-preserving copy has exactly the reference law
steps.body: The copy representative equals \(X(\omega_i)\) almost everywhere. Product-coordinate evaluation pushes \(Q^{\otimes N}\) to \(Q\), so the pushforward composition formula proves \(\mathcal L_{Q^{\otimes N}}(C_iX)=\mathcal L_Q(X)\). The almost everywhere change of representative does not affect the law.

steps.title: Use the actual tagged joint pair as a coupling
steps.body:
On the product space couple the actual pair \((\Theta^N,X_i^N)\) with the genuine iid copy of \((\theta,X)\). Both are \(L^2\), so the coupling has finite cost. The joint-pair norm bound gives

\[W_2(\mathcal L(\Theta^N,X_i^N),\mathcal L(\theta,X))\le\|\Theta^N-\theta\|_2+\|X_i^N-X_i\|_2.\]

Finiteness is established before converting the extended transport value to a real number.

steps.title: Retain the true Brownian input in the final law theorem
steps.body:
The joint pair \((\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N})\) has finite second moment, and each reference copy has exactly the actual law of \(Y_t=(\theta_t,X_t)\). Their constructed joint distribution is an admissible coupling. The pair L² norm is at most the sum of its coordinate norms, giving

\[ W_2\!\left(\mathcal L(\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N}),\mathcal L(\theta_t,X_t)\right) \le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N},\qquad 0\le t\le T. \]

The final endpoint retains the particle integral equation, the exact iid initial law and the actual Brownian input alongside this bound. The Wasserstein distance is proved finite before converting it to a real number. This proves convergence of actual tagged one-time laws; pathwise strong-SDE, expected path-supremum and gradient-flow PDE statements remain outside the formalized result.

The named particle input is the copied latent-only Brownian input plus the separately scaled parameter Brownian input. The final existential theorem retains that exact input and the actual empirical-gradient integral equation, while the tagged coupling converts the previously proved coordinate estimate to the displayed law bound for every \(N\), tag and time.

ProximalLangevin/Check.lean.title: Kernel-checked declaration and axiom audit
ProximalLangevin/Check.lean.summary: This module imports the proximal development and asks Lean to print the axioms used by its principal analytic, algorithmic and stochastic declarations. It is an audit entry point rather than a new mathematical assumption.

steps.title: Rebuild the theorems and inspect their dependency axioms
steps.body: Run lake build ProximalLangevin +ProximalLangevin.Check from the repository root. Each #print axioms command reports the dependency closure of an already checked declaration, including proximal optimality, the three actual algorithm bounds, Brownian coupling and mean-field constructions. The file introduces no new theorem or definition. The audit complements compilation; it does not strengthen any theorem’s stated assumptions or turn conditional scalar statements into algorithm convergence results.

ProximalLangevin.lean.title: Proximal Langevin library entry point
ProximalLangevin.lean.summary: The root module gathers proximal calculus, actual particle algorithms, corrected original-center bounds and constructed mean-field comparisons into one importable Lean library. Its imported theorems retain their exact assumptions and scope.

steps.title: Follow the imported proof families and reproduce the build
steps.body: Importing ProximalLangevin makes the checked public development available. The mathematical chain is true proximal minimization, residual/Moreau calculus, exact algorithm identities, genuine finite-moment Gaussian laws, concentration and transport, then the original-center comparison. The splitting chain additionally constructs Brownian stationarity and orthogonality; the mean-field branch constructs continuous \(L^2\) integral equations and actual iid comparisons. Run lake build ProximalLangevin +ProximalLangevin.Check. This umbrella has no local declarations; its proof content is in the linked imported modules.
